blocks.text: The arrivals targets come straight from the growth model, while the jobs and other Tier 1 targets wait for baselines that do not yet exist.

Baselines are fixed at 2025, the growth model's base year, for the growth-model indicators and at FY2024/25 for the airport series, the recovery baseline used in Chapter 1. Targets follow two paths: the base case, which assumes Wesgro's current activity continues with hub carriers adding capacity, and the accelerated case, which adds direct India and China routes and dedicated activation (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p19). The model prints the base case for 2028, 2030, 2032, 2034 and 2035, and the other paths for 2035 only. The 2031 base value and the accelerated milestones are computed and marked as such.

blocks.message: Arrivals carry targets on both paths; spend carries the working analysis's base path; jobs and the other Tier 1 indicators set baselines first.

blocks.text: **Arrivals.** The model's 2025 base and the airport series measure different things: arrivals on the growth model's basis, which Skift is to confirm (section 1.1), and international passenger arrivals at Cape Town International. The airport series is the quarterly proxy because ACSA publishes it, and it stood at 1.44m in FY24/25 and 1.57m in FY25/26 (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p11). Both are reported, each against its own history.

**Wesgro's targets.** Wesgro's FY26 to FY30 plan sets five-year levels for four indicators (Wesgro, Strategic Plan 2025/26 to 2029/30, p20). T2-09 counts first-time scheduled international routes toward its 10 by FY30 (Wesgro, Strategic Plan 2025/26 to 2029/30, p59). It tests each on load factor and survival. T2-11 counts calls toward 250, about 50 a year. T2-02 counts bids secured toward 161, about 32 a year at about R28m each, against 36 at about R20.7m each in 2024/25 (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p36; computed). T3-37 counts trade engagements toward 12,500, about 2,500 a year and flat on FY24. Wesgro's 800,000 to 1 million new arrivals runs above every modelled path to 2030 (section 1.1), so T1-01 keeps the model's targets and reports Wesgro's beside them.

**Spend.** T1-03's path holds spend per arrival fixed, so its targets are in constant 2024 rand, while SA Tourism reports nominal rand; progress is read after deflating by CPI. The model's 2024 spend of R27.12bn sits 19% above the R22.7bn SA Tourism reported for FY2024 (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p10, p24). [Open item: Skift to rebase the spend path on the FY2025 actual of R25.9bn.]

**Jobs.** No deliverable carries a provincial tourism employment baseline, and the Pero tourism table could not be retrieved [provincial tourism employment baseline: Wesgro Research to supply from the Pero 2025 or the Stats SA provincial TSA]. T1-04 therefore carries no baseline or modelled path until the labour analysis sets a provincial measure (I18).

The report restates the 300,000 as a total-sector figure for the labour analysis to test (I18). For context, public sources put direct tourism employment at 106,707 in Cape Town in 2024 (City of Cape Town, Economic Value of Tourism, 2025) and 953,981 nationally in 2024 (Stats SA Tourism Satellite Account, provisional, as reported in 2026). The City's framework counts about 45,000 direct and 150,000 total tourism jobs in Cape Town (City of Cape Town, Tourism Development Framework 2019 to 2024, p3). Its direct count probably rests on a narrower definition than the 106,707; the labour analysis reconciles the two.

**Green season.** The 2025 month table sums to 104.9%. Normalised, it gives 61.9% for October to March and 38.1% for the green season, in line with the printed 61% and 39% for 2024 (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p12; Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p32). T1-05 uses 38.1% as its baseline.

**Spread and community spend.** No deliverable prints district visitor spend. The Provincial Treasury's district reviews print tourist spend as a share of GDPR, from 6.7% in the Metro to 16.8% on the West Coast in 2023 (Municipal Economic Review and Outlook 2024/25, Cape Metro, p72; Municipal Economic Review and Outlook 2024/25, West Coast, p131). The share outside the Metro therefore has no baseline until the data protocol delivers one (I16), and T1-06 carries no interim level. The community share starts from the Inclusion Plan's traced floor; its 1% is a reference point the plan prints, not a target any party has adopted (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p5).
